analysis.one_liner: Requires regular and surprise FDA inspections of infant formula plants and early shortage warnings from manufacturers.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee or floor vote before Congress ended in January 2023, despite 87 cosponsors, all Democrats.
analysis.plain_summary: After the 2022 infant formula shortages, this bill would have required the FDA to inspect every formula plant at least every six months, including at least one unannounced inspection each year, and to force a full safety audit after any serious finding. Manufacturers would have had to tell the FDA within five business days about any circumstances that could cause a shortage, and during shortages the FDA could demand inventory and shipment information. It also wrote into law that food, including formula, is a critical material under the Defense Production Act, giving the President standing authority to direct production during shortages.
analysis.who_benefits: Parents who rely on infant formula, especially families of babies with allergies or medical conditions who need specialty and medical formula and have few substitutes. The bill would have given them earlier warning of shortages and stronger safety oversight of a small number of plants that produce most of the nation's supply. It would also have created a public list of facilities that could be converted to make formula during shortages.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Parents and babies who depend on formula

how_it_helps.text: Requires the FDA to inspect every infant formula manufacturing facility at least every six months, including at least one unannounced inspection per year, even at plants with no record of problems [S3].

Forces a comprehensive food safety audit with root cause analysis, enhanced testing, and environmental sampling after any notable regulatory finding, and increases audit frequency where problems persist [S3].

Requires manufacturers to report circumstances that could lead to a shortage within five business days, with fines for violations, and lets the FDA demand inventory, shipment, and capacity information during a shortage [S3].

Establishes in statute that food, including infant formula and its ingredients, is a critical material essential to national defense under the Defense Production Act, giving the President standing authority to prioritize and expand production during shortages [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Infant formula manufacturers, a small group of large companies that produce most of the U.S. supply. They would bear the cost of twice-yearly and surprise inspections, mandatory audits after findings, five-year retrospective microbial test disclosures, and shortage reporting, and they would face fines for failing to disclose shortage risks.

drawbacks.text: The bill would have added significant compliance costs to a concentrated industry, and manufacturers could pass some of those costs on to families through higher formula prices [S3].

Making food a Defense Production Act 'critical material' is a broad new authority with little precedent; critics could argue it invites government-directed production decisions in peacetime that suppliers did not plan for [S3].
The five-business-day shortage notice and inventory reporting requirements could discourage candid internal discussion of supply problems if manufacturers fear fines [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety and early-warning provisions are modest, targeted measures aimed at a product that infants depend on entirely, where a single plant failure caused nationwide shortages in 2022. The main honest cost is compliance expense in an industry with only a handful of major producers, which could nudge prices up; the Defense Production Act provision is the broadest part and went beyond what the shortage strictly required. On balance the benefits to families plausibly outweigh the costs, but the bill never got far enough for that weighing to be tested in committee.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to four House committees, and none of them ever acted on it, so it died at the end of the Congress without a single vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro introduced the bill on June 3, 2022, during the infant formula shortage, with 87 original cosponsors, all Democrats [S3].
It was referred to four committees at once — Energy and Commerce, Financial Services, Education and Labor, and Agriculture — with consideration timing left to the Speaker [S5].
No committee took further action, and no floor vote ever occurred before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The infant formula manufacturers are better off because the bill died: no plant faced a requirement for twice-yearly and unannounced inspections, mandatory audits after findings, or fines for failing to flag shortage risks. Parents got no new federal safety or early-warning protections.

for.name: Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require regular and unannounced FDA inspections of formula plants and early shortage warnings from manufacturers [S1].

for.name: 87 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill on the day it was introduced [S4].

against.name: Frank Pallone
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee, the first stop for the bill, never held a markup or took any recorded action on it after referral [S5].

against.name: Nancy Pelosi
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to four committees at once, splitting its provisions among them, and never brought it to the House floor for a vote [S5].

sides.party_line_note: All 87 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsor is recorded; the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call shows where the parties stood [S4].

industries.note: The bill would have imposed twice-yearly and unannounced inspections, mandatory audits after findings, 15-year microbial test disclosures, shortage notices within five business days, and fines. Their interest in avoiding these costs ran directly against families' interest in safer, more reliably stocked formula.
The five-business-day shortage notice requirement applied to essential medical foods as well as formula, covering makers of products that medically fragile infants depend on.
